text:
**Plan on about 300 W of solar to refill a 1,000 Wh station in one sunny day.** 200 W takes about a day and a half, and 400 W leaves margin for clouds or winter.

## The formula

**Panel watts ≈ battery Wh ÷ (peak sun hours × 0.7 to 0.75)**

- **Peak sun hours** are not daylight hours. They are the day's sunlight counted as hours of full noon sun. Most of the US averages about 4 to 5. Winter in the northern states drops to about 2 to 2.5, and summer or the Southwest reaches about 6. ([Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station))
- **0.7 to 0.75** accounts for real-world losses: hot panels, imperfect angle, and wiring and charge-controller losses. A panel usually delivers only 60 to 80% of its rated watts. ([Enough Watts](https://enoughwatts.com/guides/how-much-solar-to-recharge), [Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/))

## What that means for 1,000 Wh

| Panel | Daily output (4.5 sun hrs) | Time to refill from empty |
|---|---|---|
| 100 W | ~315 Wh | ~3 days |
| 200 W | ~630 Wh | ~1.5 days |
| 300 W | ~950 Wh | ~1 day |
| 400 W | ~1,260 Wh | under a day |

For a full refill in one day ([power-runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/), [Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)):
- Summer (5 to 6 sun hours): about 230 to 300 W
- Average day (4 sun hours): about 340 W
- Northern winter (2 sun hours): about 700 W or more

A quick rule of thumb is to divide the battery's Wh by 5. For 1,000 Wh, that gives 200 W, which refills it in about a day and a half ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).

## Check your station's specs first

1. **Maximum solar input (watts).** Panel watts above this limit don't charge any faster. A station capped at 200 W can't use a 400 W panel's full output. A somewhat larger panel still helps in weak light, because it reaches the cap earlier in the day and holds it longer.
2. **Input voltage range.** The panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc) must stay inside the station's range. Panels wired in series add their voltages together. Going over the limit can damage the station.
3. **Connector.** Panels usually use MC4 plugs, while stations typically use XT60 or barrel jacks, so you may need an adapter.

If you're running things off the station while it charges, your power use comes out of the solar input, so a full refill takes longer.
